articles.title: DHS sued over guidance restricting training program for international students
articles.summary: The Association of American Universities and other organizations have filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security over its revised guidance restricting the Curricular Practical Training (CPT) program for international students. The plaintiffs allege that DHS unlawfully narrowed the CPT program, which allows international students to engage in off-campus work related to their field of study.
articles.insight:
This news signals potential tightening of U.S. work-integrated learning pathways for international students, which may dampen U.S. appeal—especially among career-focused applicants from Asia and Latin America—though broader demand trends remain influenced by multiple factors including tuition, post-study work rights, and geopolitical perceptions.  
Admissions teams should track CPT litigation outcomes and DHS policy updates closely, while benchmarking how peer institutions in the UK, Australia, and New Zealand are positioning their own internship and placement support to highlight comparative advantages in employability.

articles.title: Australia: New rules now in force for accompanying dependants and onshore student visa applications
articles.summary: The Australian government has implemented new restrictions on Subclass 500 student visas, effective from 2 October 2026, applying to all applications lodged on or after that date. These changes include tightened rules for accompanying dependants and onshore student visa applications, as first announced on 17 September 2026.
articles.insight:
Australia’s tightened student visa rules for dependants and onshore applications may dampen appeal for family-sponsored or pathway-focused applicants from key markets like India and China, though broader demand shifts will depend on implementation clarity and concurrent policy adjustments elsewhere.  
Admissions teams should track real-time application and enrolment data from Australian institutions, monitor competitor messaging around visa stability, and assess whether their own support services—especially for dependent visas and onshore transitions—need refinement in light of evolving regional policy trends.

articles.title: Trump administration proposes $70,000 OPT fee
articles.summary: The Trump administration proposed a $70,000 fee for U.S. universities to recommend each international student for Optional Practical Training (OPT). Institutions would also face additional annual fees for OPT extensions.
articles.insight:
This proposed $70,000 OPT recommendation fee—though unlikely to pass unchanged—signals heightened U.S. regulatory scrutiny of international student pathways and could dampen institutional willingness to sponsor OPT, indirectly affecting U.S. appeal versus competitor destinations with more stable post-study work policies.  
Admissions teams should track the proposal’s legislative progress and concurrent shifts in U.S. visa approval rates, while benchmarking how peer institutions in the UK, Australia, and New Zealand are positioning their post-study work offerings to reassure students amid growing policy uncertainty.

articles.title: Harvard, Stanford among 9 US universities in fraud probe over visas for foreign researchers
articles.summary: The Trump administration has launched an investigation into nine U.S. universities—including Harvard, Yale, Stanford, and MIT—for alleged fraud related to the J-1 visa program used by foreign researchers and scholars. The probe focuses on potential misuse or misrepresentation in the administration of these visas.
articles.insight:
This probe into J-1 visa administration at elite U.S. institutions may indirectly affect international student perceptions of U.S. visa reliability and institutional trustworthiness, though its direct impact on F-1 student visas remains unclear and likely limited in the near term.  
Admissions teams should monitor official guidance from U.S. immigration authorities and track sentiment shifts in key source markets—especially among STEM researchers and their advisors—while ensuring transparent, compliant visa support processes remain a recruitment differentiator.
